meanings.note: Central setting: مدرسة الروابي للبنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls').

examples.trans: The school is close to our house.
I like going to school early.

meanings.note: Two essential senses: 'happen' (اللي صار 'what happened') and 'become / turn into' (صارت كابوس، صار الوقت).

examples.trans: Tell me what happened exactly.
It's time we head to class.

meanings.note: Mariam contrasts her old love of school with المدرسة صارت كابوس إلي ('school became a nightmare for me').

examples.trans: I had a nightmare yesterday.
The exam was like a nightmare.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative base taking pronoun endings: إلي (to me), إلك (to you), إلها (to her), إلنا (for us), إلهم (to them).

examples.trans: This book is for you.
Tell me the truth.

meanings.note: Elative form placed before a definite plural noun (أهم القيم 'the most important values').

examples.trans: This is the most important topic today.
Honesty is the most important thing.

meanings.note: Plural القيم ('values / moral principles') is a favorite word of Principal Ms. Faten.

examples.trans: Respect is an important value at school.
Our most important value is honesty.

meanings.note: Expresses location (عند باب الساحة), movement toward someone with لـ (لعندي 'up to me'), and possession (عندي وقت 'I have time', عنا 'we have').

examples.trans: I have class right now.
Come over to me for a moment.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (formal هنا).

examples.trans: Come sit here next to me.
Life is very sweet here.

meanings.note: Agrees in feminine singular واضحة with inanimate plurals like القيم ('the values are clear').

examples.trans: The rules at school are clear.
The difference between the story and the truth is clear.

meanings.note: Invariable modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (لازم نتحمل، مش لازم نلفت نظرهم).

examples.trans: We have to go to class now.
We mustn't talk loudly.

meanings.note: Covers enduring mistreatment (يتحمل الظلم) and taking responsibility (نتحمل المسؤولية).

examples.text: ما بقدر أتحمل أكتر من هيك.
examples.trans: I can't put up with more than this.
We must take responsibility.

meanings.note: Pairs naturally with تحمل ('take/bear responsibility': نتحمل المسؤولية).

examples.trans: Every student has a responsibility.
You must take responsibility for your words.

meanings.note: The main Levantine verb for 'talk / say / tell', far more common in Amman than تكلم.

examples.trans: Who told you the news?
Tell me what happened with you.

meanings.note: Both the moral virtue 'honesty' and 'the truth' when speaking (بحكي الصدق).

examples.trans: Honesty is among the most important values.
I am telling the truth.

meanings.note: Used in measured speech like Ms. Faten's بظن صار الوقت ('I think the time has come').

examples.trans: I think she is right.
I thought you were home.

meanings.note: Versatile noun: ما عندي وقت ('no time'), صار الوقت ('it's time'), وقتها ('at that moment / then'), مش وقته ('not the time for it').

examples.trans: I didn't have time to explain.
Everything is nice in its own time.

meanings.note: Definite الحقيقة refers to what actually happened behind appearances.

examples.trans: Everyone must know the truth.
The truth will come out soon.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, أي asks 'which?' (أي موضوع؟) or strengthens negation ('not any' -> أي إشي).

examples.trans: Which class are you in?
I didn't make any mistake.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine indefinite person word; ما حدا means 'nobody'.

examples.trans: Is anyone in the classroom?
Nobody believed me.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings مني (from me), منها (of/from her), منكم (of you): تكون من شلتها ('be part of her clique'), بخاف منها ('afraid of her').

examples.trans: I got off the bus.
Which one of you saw what happened?

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.
See you tomorrow morning!

meanings.note: Invariable Levantine relative pronoun replacing الذي / التي / الذين and 'what' (اللي صار 'what happened').

examples.trans: The girl whom I saw is my friend.
Tell me what happened.

meanings.note: Polite 'yes' to a teacher (نعم يا مس), or a sharp rising 'Excuse me?!' (نعم؟) when someone feels challenged.

examples.trans: Yes Miss, I'm here.
Excuse me? Repeat what you just said!

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Standard Jordanian private-school address for a female teacher or principal, used alone (يا مس) or before her first name (مس فاتن، مس عبير).

examples.trans: Yes Miss, I'm ready.
Ms. Faten is in her office now.

meanings.note: Independent first-person singular pronoun for any gender.

examples.trans: I am a student at the school.
I didn't say anything.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, كل means 'every' (كل يوم، كل إشي); with الـ (الكل) it means 'everyone'; with suffixes (كلنا، كلهم، كلها) 'all of us/them/it'.

examples.trans: Everyone knows the story.
We see each other every day.

meanings.note: Signature Jordanian/Palestinian word corresponding to formal شيء; definite form الإشي, plural أشياء.

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
Nothing happened.

meanings.note: Plural صحبات is the everyday Jordanian word for girlfriends / school friends (صحباتي، صحباتها).

examples.trans: Dina is my closest friend.
I sat with my friends in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also / too' (وأنا كمان 'and me too').

examples.trans: And my friends were there too.
I need five more minutes.

meanings.note: Answers a question negatively ('no') or forms negative commands before a second-person subjunctive verb (لا تصدقوها! 'don't believe her!').

examples.trans: No Miss, that's not true.
Don't worry, everything is fine.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: Singular غرفة (الغرفة), plural غرف (تقسيم الغرف 'room assignments').

examples.trans: We are in the same room on the trip.
The room is neat and spacious.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine adjective taking an indefinite plural noun directly: الغرفة مليانة بنات ('the room is full of girls').

examples.trans: The courtyard is full of students.
My bag is full of books.

meanings.note: Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Construes with على for testifying to a claim (شهدوا على إشي واحد).

examples.trans: I testified truthfully in front of the principal.
All the girls testified for her.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings: علي (on/about me), عليكي (to you, f.), عليها (to her), علينا (on/for us), عليكم (on you, pl.). Often contracts to عـ before الـ.

examples.trans: Count on me in this matter.
They lied about me in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: After a noun, means 'one' (إشي واحد، سؤال واحد، إيد واحدة); with الـ (الواحد) it is the everyday impersonal subject 'a person / one'.

examples.trans: A person has to tell the truth.
I have just one question.

meanings.note: Spoken feminine singular 'you', spelled with final ي to reflect the Jordanian pronunciation inti.

examples.trans: Are you a new girl here?
What do you think?

meanings.note: Levantine 'want' built from بد- plus pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بدنا (we want).

examples.trans: What do you want to do now?
I wanted to talk with you.

meanings.note: Form II verb (saddaq, written here with shadda to distinguish it from the noun صدق 'honesty'): أصدقك ('believe you'), لا تصدقوها ('don't believe her').

examples.trans: You have to believe me, Miss.
Nobody believed her lie.

meanings.note: With suffixes, acts as the Levantine reflexive ('myself/themselves': حالهم), 'alone' (لحالك), and 'one's own business' (خليكم بحالكم).

examples.trans: I studied the lesson by myself.
Leave me to myself, please.

meanings.note: Versatile Levantine word meaning 'but' between clauses and 'only / just' inside a clause.
As a focus adverb before a verb, noun, or imperative, بس narrows or softens the statement.

examples.trans: I tried to speak, but she didn't hear me.
I just want one minute.

meanings.note: Active participle of سمع used for immediate perception: ما حدا سامعني ('nobody hears me').

examples.trans: Do you hear me well?
I hear a sound outside.

meanings.note: Appears in everyday speech mainly in fixed polite phrases like إلى اللقاء! ('Until next time!').

examples.trans: Until next time, girls!
We reached the end of the lesson.

meanings.note: Used in the warm standard farewell إلى اللقاء! ('Until we meet again! / Until next time!').

examples.trans: Until next time soon!
It was a very nice meeting.
